list.listitem: Rabies infects only mammals and is most commonly transmitted by raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes in the United States.
Worldwide, dog bites and scratches cause 99% of human rabies cases.

Clinical diagnosis can be made in patients with encephalitis and a history of a bite from a known rabid animal. Suspected cases should undergo testing of their saliva, serum, and CSF as well as neck biopsy. C
Rabies is almost invariably fatal after neurological symptoms develop. B
Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is effective for the prevention of rabies. B
Ribavirin is available as an investigational protocol for human rabies cases. C

background.definition: Rabies is a preventable viral disease of mammals most often transmitted via rabid animal bites. Most cases in the United States occur in wild animals: raccoons, skunks, bats, coyotes, and foxes. Domestic animal cases occur in cats, dogs, cattle, and other livestock. Human rabies is rare; most cases in the United States are due to bat bites (71%).

list.listitem: Human rabies: 0.001 per 100,000 per year. 1 to 3 cases annually in the Unites States.

Fifty-seven cases of human rabies have been reported in the United States since 2000, with three people surviving. There were five cases in 2021, four due to bat exposure and one due to a dog exposure occurring outside of the United States. Fourteen cases were from infections acquired outside of the U.S. and its territories.,

Animal rabies in the United States: 3,663 cases reported in 2021, a decrease from the 4,479 reported in 2020. Wild animals account for >90% of reported cases, with bats and raccoons reported most often, followed by skunks and foxes. Rabid cats, cattle, and dogs accounted for 94% of rabies cases involving domestic animals.
Only state free of rabies: Hawaii.
Approximately 60,000 people are treated for rabies exposure annually in the Unites States.
$560 million annually spent on PEP in the United States.
59,000 deaths worldwide annually.
Most commonly effects children age <15 years old.
95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia,.
Canine rabies commonly seen outside of the United States, Mexico and Canada; accounts for 99% of cases worldwide.
Two types of exposure: bite and nonbite.
Bite exposure: penetration by teeth from potentially rabid animal. 50 times greater risk of rabies via bite compared to scratch.
Nonbite exposure: contamination of open wounds, abrasions, mucous membranes, or scratches with saliva/neural tissue from potentially rabid animal.
Other nonbite exposure: aerosol transmission of virus in laboratories and organ transplants from donors infected with rabies.
Single-stranded RNA virus of the genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae
Virus deposits in wound from bite or saliva.
Retrograde passage to CNS, where it replicates.
Spreads to salivary glands, heart, and other organs.
Induces acute neurological symptoms followed by coma and death.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Professions with exposure to wild and domestic animals (animal control officers, laboratory workers, veterinarians, spelunkers)
Travel to countries with endemic rabies
Wound from rabid animal with proximity to CNS (face, neck)

list.listitem: Preexposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended for groups at high risk of exposure and is effective for rabies prevention. B
Animal studies have shown that cleansing wounds with soap and water plus povidone iodine is effective in markedly reducing the likelihood of rabies. B
PEP, i.e. prompt use of rabies vaccine with proper wound washing and management and simultaneous administration of RIG, when indicated, is almost 100% effective in preventing rabies.
Prevention consists of pre- and postexposure prophylaxis.

Preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is recommended for rabies laboratory/biologics workers, animal control workers and veterinarians, spelunkers, and travelers to enzootic areas with little access to health care.
PrEP dosages: Two doses of 1.0 mL of vaccine intramuscular (IM) on days 0 and 7 OR two doses of 0.1 mL of vaccine intradermal (ID) on days 0 and 7.

For adults and children ≥ 2 years, the deltoid is the preferred IM site. For children < 2 years, the anterolateral thigh is recommended. The recommended sites for ID administration are the deltoid, anterolateral thigh or suprascapular area.
A recent randomized, controlled trial of 288 individuals showed non-inferiority of a single IM dose PrEP to the standard two dose regimen in adults up to 50 years old.
Postexposure prophylaxis in individuals who received PrEP consists of wound care and rabies vaccine alone without rabies immunoglobulin. If exposure does occur, vaccine is given on days 0 and 3.
Canine vaccination programs in Central/South America reduced human rabies by more than 95% and canine rabies by more than 98%.

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended for persons exposed to rabid or suspected rabid domestic animals (cats, dogs, cattle) or wild animals (racoons, skunks, foxes, bats). All other exposures should be discussed with public health officials first. PEP consists of rabies vaccine and for unvaccinated persons, rabies immune globulin (RIG). It is extremely effective if given within 5 days; there are no known failures in the United States.

WHO-defined exposure categories are as follows ( ,
Category I: Touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin Category II: Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding Category III: Single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, contamination of mucous membrane or broken skin with saliva from animal licks, or any exposure due to direct contact with bats whether or not an injury is scene.
CDC/ACIP recommendations are consistent with those of WHO. They also recommend a 5th vaccination at 28 days for immunocompromised individuals.

Rabies vaccine dosage (1.0 mL IM) is given in the deltoid on days 0, 3, 7, and 14. Response takes 7 to 10 days to develop and lasts ≥2 years. Adverse vaccine reactions include pain, redness, and swelling at vaccination site.
RIG dosages (20 IU/kg human or equine RIG) are infiltrated directly into and around wound. RIG immunity lasts approximately 21 days.

No cases of viruses/infectious agents transmitted via RIG are known in the United States. Common reactions to RIG include local pain and fever with low risk of allergic reaction, but higher risk exists with equine RIG.

Intradermal route regimens reduce volume and direct cost of vaccine by 60-80% compared with intramuscular injection, and are preferred in resource-limited settings and in locations with a high volume of newly exposed individuals.

A clinical trial of 500 healthy volunteers showed that an intradermal 2-dose regimen given on days 0 and 7 did not elicit less of an immune response compared with a 3-dose regimen given over the course of a month.

No loss of neutralizing antibody response was noted to the rabies vaccination among 103 previously unimmunized individuals taking the antimalarial medications doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil or chloroquine.
Clinical diagnosis can be made in patients with encephalitis and a history of a bite from a known rabid animal. C
Rule out common causes of viral encephalitis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. C
Suspected cases should undergo testing of their saliva, serum, and CSF as well as neck biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No fever; no edematous innoculation site
Tetanus prone wound, stiff neck, opisthotonus, risus sardonicus, rigid abdomen
Sore throat, high fever; no bite history
Tremors, hallucinations, seizures, alcohol misuse history; no bite history

list.listitem: Five stages: incubation, prodrome, acute neurologic, coma, and death.
Incubation: 1 to 3 months, but up to 8 years; median length 85 days.
Prodrome: nonspecific, flu-like symptoms; some pain, swelling, and paresthesias at innoculation site lasting 3 to 7 days.
Acute neurologic: encephalytic (furious) or paralytic (dumb), or atypical rabies lasting for 3 to 7 days.

Encephalytic: most common (80%); presents with generalized arousal or hyperexcitability, hypersalivation, piloerection, aerophobia, hydrophobia, muscle spasms, and rarely cardiac arrhythmias, myocarditis.
Paralytic: presents with paresis in the infected extremity progressing to quadriparesis, urinary and fecal incontinence; Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Atypical: presents with pain, seizures, sensory/motor deficits, and cranial nerve palsies; rare, common with bat rabies.
Coma: rapid progression to flaccid paralysis, respiratory, and vascular collapse.
Death: within days of coma, but can be up to 2 weeks.
No diagnostic test can confirm rabies prior to symptom onset. Negative tests in symptomatic patients do not exclude rabies.
Saliva: tested for rabies virus RNA via real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and viral culture.
Neck biopsy: posterior neck skin tested for viral antigen via RT-PCR and immunofluorescence. Gold standard.
Brain biopsy rarely performed antemortem.
Serum: tested for rabies virus antibodies via immunofluorescence; diagnostic if no history of vaccination/immunoglobulin administration.
CSF: tested similarly to serum; presence of antibodies diagnostic regardless of prior vaccination/immunoglobulin administration. May not be elevated early in illness.
Suspect rabies in patients with encephalitis and history of animal bite. Diagnosis is more difficult if bite history or bite is unrecognized (bat).
Rule out other causes of encephalitis (herpes, arbo/enteroviruses, Guillain-Barre syndrome).
Antemortem testing includes saliva, serum, CSF samples, and neck biopsies.
All suspected rabid animals should be observed or destroyed for brain biopsy and direct fluorescent antibody testing.
No proven effective therapies are known for human cases once symptoms present. C
Ribavirin is available as an investigational protocol for human rabies cases. C

There are no known effective therapies once symptoms develop. Supportive treatment includes pain control, sedation, and quarantine measures. Administration of RIG and/or rabies vaccine is not reccomended once symptoms have developed per current CDC guidelines.

Rabies Working Group recommends a combination therapy of multiple doses of rabies vaccine and RIG, ribavirin, INF-alpha, and ketamine. Rarely associated with increased survival. Steroids are to be avoided.

Milwaukee protocol associated with at least one case report of survival from rabies. Consists of: no rabies vaccine or RIG, sedation with ketamine and benzodiazepines, amantadine, aggressive ICU/supportive care. However, a review of subsequent trials of this regimen did not show any successes.
See the Secondary Prevention of this topic for details on PEP.
Washing wound with soap and water for 15 minutes plus povidone iodine decreases transmission up to 90%.
Consider tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics.
Postpone suturing wound if possible. Ensure that RIG is administered first.

Immunosuppressed individuals may have less robust immune response to PrEP and PEP. PrEP should follow the guidelines detailed in the Primary Prevention section of this topic, plus a third dose on days 21-28. Immunosuppressed persons who are at risk for rabies should have their virus-neutralizing antibody responses checked after completing the preexposure series. For PEP, give RIG and rabies vaccine immediately if exposed. Immunosupressed individuals should receive the 5 dose regimen, on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28. Consult infectious disease specialist. No postexposure failures have been attributed to HIV.
Treat local wound in previously vaccinated individuals with rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3. Do not give RIG.
There is no documented transmission of rabies from infected patients to health care providers or household contacts.
Pre- and postexposure prophylaxis are almost universally effective in preventing rabies if begun within 5 days of exposure and adhere to the recommended protocol. B
Rabies is almost uniformly fatal once neurologic symptoms begin regardless of vaccination status. B
All patients with possible exposure to rabies should be evaluated in consultation with public health authorities for PEP. C
Avoid delays in seeking care for possible or suspected rabies exposure. Postexposure prophylaxis is almost 100% effective in preventing rabies if begun within 5 days of exposure.
Rabies is almost uniformly fatal once neurologic symptoms begin regardless of vaccination status.
PEP is not contraindicated in elderly.
PEP is not contraindicated in pregnant women. There is no evidence of fetal anomalies with rabies vaccine/RIG.
PEP is not contraindicated in children.
Vaccine should be injected into the deltoid muscle for children aged 2 years and more. The anterolateral thigh is recommended for younger children.

tr.td: Touching or feeding animals, animal licks on intact skin.
As the saliva has not entered the bloodstream there is no exposure in these cases.
Washing of exposed skin surfaces, no post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding.
As there is a break in the skin and a potential of rabies virus introduction into the patient's blood stream, this is an “exposure.”

Wound washing and immediate vaccination. IM injection of deltoid on days 0, 3, 7 and 14. Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) not indicated. If previously immunized, IM injection of deltoid on days 0 and 3, RIG is not indicated.

Single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches including the contamination of mucous membrane or broken skin with saliva from animal licks. This includes any bat encounter with or without known bite or scratch

Exposure due to direct contact; this is categorized as a “severe exposure.” Bat bites or scratches are not readily visible or detectable; therefore, exposures involving physical contact with a bat should be treated as a severe exposure.

Wound washing and immediate vaccination: IM injection deltoid on days 0, 3, 7, and14. HRIG administration is indicated. If previously immunized, then IM injection deltoid on days 0 and 3. RIG is not indicated.
